title: Glossary rows 35 and 36 define 'highest root' and 'root poset' by facts of simply laced boards, false on B, C, F, G
location: site/src/content/pages/glossary.mdx:318-323 (row 35, dfn highest-root) and :326-331 (row 36, dfn root-poset); route /glossary/#highest-root, #root-poset (preview and release); linked from M1 beats 3 and 4 and M2
claim: The glossary drops M1's hypothesis ('a board of finite type with single roads', E8) and defines 'highest root' as 'On a board of finite type, the root population at which no mutation raises any city.' It defines 'root poset' as 'The positive root populations of a board, arranged by total population, with an edge from one to another wherever a mutation raises a city.' On B, C, F, G the first picks out two populations and the second is not the root poset.
expected: SPEC 2.6: 'Highest root theta: the root population of largest form value that no mutation raises; unique [V]'. F13: on B, C, F, G, Kostant's game from a short node ends at the highest short root. SPEC 4 T2 and 2.16 call the raising-edge picture the Hasse diagram of the root poset only 'on a simply laced board of finite type'.
observed: Oracle (redteam-RT-09-p6-oracle.py): the root populations raised by no mutation are two on each board: B2 (1,1),(1,2); B3 (1,1,1),(1,2,2); C3 (1,2,1),(2,2,1); F4 (1,2,3,2),(2,3,4,2); G2 (2,1),(3,2). The highest short root satisfies the glossary's definition of the highest root. On B2 the raising edges are (1,0)->(1,2) (a rise of 2) and (0,1)->(1,1), while the root poset's covering relations are (1,0)<(1,1), (0,1)<(1,1), (1,1)<(1,2). On G2 the raising edges include (0,1)->(3,1).

Both tests fail at the assertion that quotes the definition (source, no build needed). Oracle values: python3 redteam/RT-09/redteam-RT-09-p6-oracle.py reference.

title: The glossary defines the highest root by a rule that also gives the highest short root on 16 of the 32 boards of finite type
claim: The new definition reads 'On a board of finite type, the root population at which no mutation raises any city.' On B_n, C_n, F4 and G2 two root populations satisfy this: the highest root and the highest short root. A reader who applies the rule as written can call the highest short root 'the highest root'.
expected: SPEC 2.7 and 4 T9 distinguish the highest root from the highest short root (T9: 'the highest root, or the highest short root after a start at a short city'). The rule is unique only on simply laced boards, which is the context of M1 beat 3, where the sentence was first used for E8.
observed: Oracle (lie_games.mutate on cartan(letter,n) over roots): B3 gives [(1,2,2), (1,1,1)]; C3 gives [(1,2,1), (2,2,1)]; F4 gives [(2,3,4,2), (1,2,3,2)]; G2 gives [(2,1), (3,2)]. In all, 16 of 32 boards have two such roots. On /atlas/B3/ the highest root is (1,2,2) and (1,1,1) is named the highest short root.

specRef: SPEC 2.7; 4 T9 ('the highest root, or the highest short root after a start at a short city'); 8.4 'Define every term'; RED-TEAM-COMMON 4 ('a mathematical statement presented as fact that is wrong')

title: Glossary row 64 says the shape of a Wythoff polytope depends only on which nodes are ringed; SPEC says its combinatorics

refute.citation: SPEC.md 8.4 bullet 1: 'Define every term on first use and link later uses to a glossary entry'. SPEC 9.2: for a lesson '(M10 is reference pages and has none); it follows the writing rules of section 8.4'. SPEC 3 M10. The passage supports the finding's expected.
refute.evidence: 9.2 exempts M10 only from predictions and challenges ('M10 is reference pages and has none'). The same sentence then says it 'follows the writing rules of section 8.4', and 8.4 bullet 1 has no qualifier. 8.4 is not [D], and no section 10 default touches it (D14 covers house style 'as proposed'). Records: 'MERGE: P6 stage 6.3, P6-A7 (M9) and P6-A8 (M10 and the glossary)' sends to P6-terms 'the same later-use rule as a shared spec over every lesson M0 to M9 and the reference pages'. 'P6-terms: the shared spec glossary-later-uses.spec.ts' and 'MERGE: P6-terms ...' name the 15 routes (M0 to M9 and history, confusions, open-problem, not-quiver-mutation, about). None of these says M10 is exempt. They only leave it out of the scope. P6-A8's anatomy entry (no beats, no Seen box, no sources) says nothing about glossary links. The known-and-decided list holds 'one markup for a defined term distinct from bold' and 'M10's question', neither of which covers links on later uses. I read m10-atlas.mdx at f07eec6 and counted 'board' in its glossary sense 8 times in the figcaption and hub items, 9 with the question. 'finite type' appears 2 times, 'numbers game' 2 times (glossary item and credit line) and 'Kostant's game' 2 times (history item and credit line). The file imports no Term helper. Nothing in the record contradicts the finding's observed.
refute.reason: not refuted: R1 failed, because 8.4 bullet 1 is unqualified and 9.2 binds M10 to 8.4 while exempting it only from predictions and challenges; R2 failed, because the finding reads 8.4 and 9.2 correctly; R3 failed, because M10 is phase 6, at G6; R4 does not apply; R5 failed, because 8.4 is not [D], there is no section 10 default, and MERGE's P6-terms scope leaves M10 out without a recorded exemption; R6 failed, because nothing is on record (first phase 6 round, no gate-G6 open item). A broken prose rule of 8.4 is major, so no adjustment.
